paragraphs.text:
A material's electrical conductivity describes its ability to conduct electric current.
Conductors have many mobile charged particles.
An electric field can produce a directed motion of these particles, so current can form relatively easily.

The textbook also calls insulators dielectrics.
Under ordinary operating conditions, they have very few freely mobile charged particles, so the current is usually small even when there is a potential difference across them.

This describes their behavior under ordinary conditions.
At sufficiently high voltage, an insulator can undergo electrical breakdown and conduct a much larger current.

The classification into conductors and insulators is relative.
An insulator is not a material that conducts no current under every possible condition.

Amber, porcelain, glass, rubber, paraffin, and kerosene are common insulating materials.
Purity, temperature, and the environment can affect their actual behavior.

Silver and copper are metals with good electrical conductivity.
Solutions containing mobile ions can conduct current, but not all aqueous solutions conduct equally well.
An ionized gas is called a plasma, and its charged particles can also carry current.

Another important class of materials is called semiconductors.
Under particular conditions, their conductivity lies between that of good conductors and good insulators.
More importantly, their conductivity can change greatly with temperature, illumination, or the addition of small amounts of selected impurities.
One measurement showing an intermediate conductivity is not enough to classify an arbitrary material as a semiconductor.

Early in the development of semiconductor technology, many electronic and radio devices relied mainly on conductors and insulators.
The original textbook's account of the earlier limited use of semiconductors describes that stage of technological development, not their role today.

The textbook describes theoretical studies followed by experimental research into ways of controlling semiconductor conductivity.
As this understanding developed, semiconductor devices came into widespread use.
Electronics and radio technology changed significantly as a result.

Transmitting electrical energy along wires requires conductors whose conductivity suits the intended use.
Semiconductors can be made into devices that control current in radios, computers, and other equipment.
A material's use depends not only on whether it conducts, but also on whether its conductivity suits the task and meets the operating conditions.
